title: GCP IAM: Bindings, Service Accounts, and Impersonation
intro: GCP IAM is a policy of bindings, each pairing a role with a list of members, attached to an organisation, folder, project, or resource. Service accounts are identities for workloads. The modern best practice is no service account keys at all: attach accounts to resources, and impersonate them when you need to act as one.

steps.prompt: Show which roles bob@example.com has on the project shop-prod-217733.
steps.explanation: bob has Editor on all of production, plus the ability to act as any service account.
steps.why: The raw policy is one big document. --flatten/--filter/--format turns it into 'what can this person do?'. Editor is a 'basic role' that grants write access to nearly everything, and Google recommends predefined or custom roles instead.

steps.prompt: List the service accounts in the project.
steps.fake_output:
DISPLAY NAME                            EMAIL                                                  DISABLED
Compute Engine default service account  482910381204-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com     False
orders-api                              orders-api@shop-prod-217733.iam.gserviceaccount.com    False
terraform                               terraform@shop-prod-217733.iam.gserviceaccount.com     False
steps.explanation: The default compute account, plus dedicated accounts for orders-api and Terraform.
steps.why: One service account per workload means a compromise of one app exposes only that app's permissions, and audit logs show which app did what.

expected_commands: gcloud iam service-accounts keys list --iam-account orders-api@shop-prod-217733.iam.gserviceaccount.com --managed-by user
steps.explanation: A JSON key created in 2023 that never expires, probably sitting in a CI variable or on a laptop.
steps.why: A downloaded key is a long-lived password for the service account, and the most common way GCP projects get breached. Replace keys with Workload Identity (GKE), attached service accounts (VMs, Cloud Run), or Workload Identity Federation (GitHub Actions and other clouds). Organisations can block key creation with the iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation org policy.

steps.prompt: Act as the terraform service account for a single command without any key: list buckets while impersonating terraform@shop-prod-217733.iam.gserviceaccount.com.
steps.fake_output:
WARNING: This command is using service account impersonation. All API calls will be executed as [terraform@shop-prod-217733.iam.gserviceaccount.com].
gs://shop-prod-217733-tfstate/
gs://shop-prod-assets/
steps.explanation: The call ran as the Terraform account, using short-lived tokens issued to you.
steps.why: Impersonation needs roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator on that account, and every use is logged as 'alice acting as terraform'. It's the GCP equivalent of 'aws sts assume-role', and why people never need to download a key.

steps.prompt: Why can't alice@example.com delete objects in shop-prod-assets? Ask the Policy Troubleshooter about storage.objects.delete on //storage.googleapis.com/projects/_/buckets/shop-prod-assets.
steps.fake_output:
overallAccessState: CANNOT_ACCESS
explainedPolicies:
- policy: bindings on bucket shop-prod-assets
  access: NOT_GRANTED
  roles: roles/storage.objectViewer (alice@example.com) -> does not include storage.objects.delete
steps.explanation: alice only has objectViewer on the bucket.
steps.why: The Policy Troubleshooter evaluates the real policies at every level (organisation, folder, project, resource, including deny policies) for one permission, and explains the result. It's GCP's version of the AWS policy simulator.
